interview_metadata.name: Shoba Mehta
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Detroit in 1974, but my childhood was very Gujarati at home. My parents came from Gujarat before I was born, and in our house it was Gujarati, English, temple events, cousins coming over, and always somebody being fed. My father worked in auto parts supply, and my mother worked in a school cafeteria, so I saw both discipline and food service from early on. When I was a teenager in Farmington Hills, I was the one helping make chai for guests, chopping vegetables for big gatherings, and also trying to be very American, listening to pop music and going to football games. After high school I went to community college for a while, studying business classes, but I did not finish a degree because I got married young and started working. My husband Rajesh and I spent some years in the Chicago area, and that is where I really grew into food service work, first as a server, then shift lead, then kitchen supervisor. We moved back to Michigan to be closer to my parents and the Indian community here. We have two children, Maya and Neel, and raising them while working kitchen shifts taught me how to plan every hour of the day. Now I supervise a busy food service team in a healthcare dining setting. I am ServSafe certified, I manage schedules, ordering, inventory, training, and all the small crises that happen before lunch service. Outside work, I do yoga, dance with a South Asian cultural group, paint watercolors, cook Indian-fusion dishes, and stay active in the Indian Association of Greater Detroit. I feel like my life has been about taking the hospitality I grew up with and turning it into leadership.

follow_ups.question: What are some childhood memories that still shape how you run your home or workplace?
follow_ups.response: My mother would count every container before a temple potluck and label everything with masking tape. I do the same kind of thing at work now, only with inventory software and prep sheets.

follow_ups.question: When did you first feel confident leading people in a kitchen?
follow_ups.response: Probably in my late thirties, when a manager left suddenly and I had to run a holiday meal service. We got 400 plates out on time, and after that I stopped thinking of myself as just filling in.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, the biggest one was when my children were small and I had to decide whether to stay in food service or go back to school full time. I had taken some college classes, and part of me wanted to finish a business degree. But we needed steady money, and I was already getting noticed at work because I could keep calm and organize people. A district manager told me, 'You have supervisor instincts,' and suggested I get certified and move up from hourly service work. I felt guilty at first because in my family education was treated like the main path to respect. But I chose to build from the job I had. I got my ServSafe certification, learned ordering and cost sheets, and started treating the kitchen like a place where I could have a real career. That choice still defines me because I am practical, but I am also ambitious.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to before making that choice?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Rajesh and my mother. Rajesh looked at the budget with me, and my mother said work done with pride is also education.

follow_ups.question: What changed after you chose the supervisor path?
follow_ups.response: I started saying yes to closing shifts, audits, vendor calls, and training new staff. Those were not glamorous tasks, but they made managers trust me.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, but made under real-life pressure. I sat with our bills, the kids' school schedule, and my work schedule, and I chose the path that kept the household stable while still letting me grow.

follow_ups.question: Did it feel like a sacrifice?
follow_ups.response: A little, because I still wanted the degree. But it also felt like I was choosing momentum instead of waiting for a perfect time.

follow_ups.question: Do you still think about going back to school?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but now I think more about a culinary arts certificate or management training than a traditional degree.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. Affordable evening classes and better child care options would have helped a lot. My employer supported certification, but not much beyond that, so I had to piece things together myself.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Tuition help tied to food service management, and a class schedule that did not punish working parents.

follow_ups.question: Did your family fill some of that gap?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. My parents watched the kids when they could, and Rajesh took over dinner and homework on my late nights.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Rajesh, and we have been married for 27 years. He works as an IT systems analyst for an auto supplier, so his work is more desk and remote than mine. We balance each other: he is quieter and more patient, and I am the calendar person who knows every appointment, festival rehearsal, and bill due date. Our daughter Maya is 17 and finishing high school soon. She is artistic, takes advanced classes, and helps me with social media flyers for community events. Our son Neel is 14, more into robotics and basketball, and he eats constantly, so my grocery planning is very real. My parents are still nearby in the Detroit suburbs, and I check on them several times a week. Rajesh's parents are in New Jersey, and we speak with them by phone or WhatsApp. Family is not just emotional for me; it is practical. We cook together, drive each other, help with doctors, and show up for weddings, funerals, temple events, and school things.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal family dinner look like in your house?
follow_ups.response: On weeknights it is usually dal, rice, vegetables, maybe salmon or chicken for the kids, and everyone eats in shifts depending on practice or homework. Sunday is the real sit-down dinner.

follow_ups.question: Who do you rely on most day to day?
follow_ups.response: Rajesh first, then my mother for emotional advice. For practical community things, I rely on my friend Nisha.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have one younger brother, Amit, who lives in Novi with his wife and their two kids. We are close, though we tease each other a lot, and we usually see each other at least twice a month.

follow_ups.question: Do your children spend time with his children?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around holidays and summer barbecues. The cousins are different ages but still close.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Amit help with your parents together?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I handle more appointments and food, and he handles repairs, paperwork, and driving when I am working.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are from three circles: my dance group, my yoga class, and the Indian Association. Nisha is probably my closest friend; we organize Navratri volunteer schedules together and talk almost every day. I also have two work friends, Carla and Minh, who understand kitchen stress in a way other people do not. We might not go out every week, but when we do it is usually coffee, a museum visit, or trying a new restaurant. I like friendships where people show up and also tell the truth.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your dance group?
follow_ups.response: Usually once a week for rehearsal, more often before festivals. Around Navratri it can become three nights a week.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your work friends talk about outside work?
follow_ups.response: Kids, aging parents, recipes, and sometimes just laughing about the strange requests people make in food service.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Farmington, Michigan, in the 48334 area. It is suburban, leafy, and practical. We have older homes, good schools nearby, grocery stores, Indian stores within a reasonable drive, and enough diversity that my kids did not feel like they were the only Indian children in class. I like that I can get to a temple, a library, a park, and a good produce market without making a whole day of it. People keep their yards nice, but it is not flashy. It suits us because it is family-oriented and close to both work routes and community activities.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually shop nearby?
follow_ups.response: For regular groceries I use Kroger or Costco, and for spices, fresh methi, and Indian snacks I go to Patel Brothers or smaller Indian markets in the area.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: A few. We exchange vegetables from gardens, shovel sometimes, and talk at the mailbox, but it is not the kind of block where everyone is in each other's house.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe overall. I still lock everything and I do not jog alone late at night, but I am comfortable walking in the evening and letting my son bike to a friend's house nearby.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins in nearby subdivisions. Nothing violent close to us, but it made everyone more careful.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors communicate about safety?
follow_ups.response: Yes, there is a neighborhood Facebook group and a text chain for our street.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is stability, schools, and access to community. The downside is property taxes, winter driving, and sometimes feeling like everything requires a car.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there despite the costs?
follow_ups.response: The kids' schools, my parents being close, and the Indian community network.

follow_ups.question: Would you move in the future?
follow_ups.response: Maybe after the kids are settled, but I would probably stay in metro Detroit unless work took us somewhere very specific.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my husband Rajesh, our daughter Maya, and our son Neel. My mother sometimes stays overnight if my father has an early appointment nearby or if there is a festival weekend and we are cooking late, but she does not live with us. The daily household is four people. Everyone has chores, though I admit I still do more kitchen organizing than anyone else.

follow_ups.question: What chores do the kids have?
follow_ups.response: Maya loads dishes and does laundry, and Neel takes trash out, clears the table, and helps water the herbs.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone work from home?
follow_ups.response: Rajesh works from home two or three days a week. I cannot work from home, obviously, because kitchen work is hands-on.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone in the household is permanent: me, Rajesh, Maya, and Neel.

follow_ups.question: No one staying for an extended visit right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Do relatives ever stay longer during visits?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes family from India or New Jersey stays for a week or two, but not currently.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My mother occasionally stays overnight, and cousins may stay during weddings or festival weekends.

follow_ups.question: How often does your mother stay?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, depending on appointments or events.

follow_ups.question: Where do guests usually sleep?
follow_ups.response: We have a small guest room that also holds my painting supplies.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No child away at college yet?
follow_ups.response: Not yet. Maya is still in high school.

follow_ups.question: Any long work travel?
follow_ups.response: No, neither of us travels much for work.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My weekdays start around 5:15 in the morning. I make tea, check the family calendar, pack lunch or leftovers, and leave for work around 6:20 if I have an early shift. Work is usually 7 to 3:30 or 8 to 4:30, but food service is never exact. Mondays are inventory and ordering heavy, Wednesdays I often do staff schedules, and Fridays I try to clean up paperwork before the weekend. I do yoga Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday if nothing explodes. Dance rehearsal is usually Sunday afternoon. Evenings are dinner, school logistics, checking on my parents, and maybe 30 minutes reading or painting if I am lucky.

follow_ups.question: What is the most predictable part of your week?
follow_ups.response: Morning tea and calendar checking. If I skip that, the whole day feels messy.

follow_ups.question: What is the least predictable part?
follow_ups.response: Staff call-offs at work. One sick cook can change my whole day.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a first-line supervisor for food preparation and serving workers in a healthcare dining operation. It is cafeteria, patient and staff meal support, and catered meetings all mixed together. I supervise cooks, prep staff, dish room workers, and front-line servers. My main hours are daytime, about 40 to 45 hours a week, with occasional weekend coverage or early starts for special service. I do scheduling, food safety checks, temperature logs, ordering, inventory counts, coaching, and problem solving. I also help with menu ideas when we do special cultural meals.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job do you like most?
follow_ups.response: Training someone who was nervous and seeing them become reliable. I like building a strong team.

follow_ups.question: What part drains you?
follow_ups.response: Last-minute absences and having to discipline people who know better but cut corners.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help with Indian Association events, especially food coordination and volunteer scheduling. At home I manage most medical appointments for the kids and my parents. I also maintain a small herb garden with cilantro, mint, basil, and sometimes curry leaf in pots. On Sundays I do bulk prep: chopped onions, cooked dal, washed greens, and marinated protein. That is what keeps us from ordering takeout three times a week.

follow_ups.question: How much time does community volunteering take?
follow_ups.response: In a normal month maybe five hours. Before Diwali or Navratri it can be 15 or 20 hours.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually prep on Sundays?
follow_ups.response: Dal, quinoa or rice, roasted vegetables, chutney, and sometimes tandoori salmon marinade.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I added more strength work because my knees were complaining after jogging and long kitchen shifts. I still do Vinyasa yoga, but I am more careful about recovery. Maya's college applications also changed the household rhythm this past year, because there were essays, campus visits, and deadlines. At work we changed inventory software, so I spent a few weeks staying late to clean up item lists and train people.

follow_ups.question: What strength work are you doing?
follow_ups.response: Mostly light weights, squats modified for my knees, and core work from a YouTube instructor my yoga teacher recommended.

follow_ups.question: Did the new inventory software help?
follow_ups.response: Now it helps, but the transition was painful. Bad item names and old vendor codes made me crazy.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: During school, Maya leaves around 7:20 and Neel around 7:35. Maya has classes, art club, and sometimes helps with cultural association design work. Neel has school, robotics club, and basketball practice in season. They come home at different times, so snacks are important. Homework happens after dinner for Neel and before dinner for Maya if she is being disciplined. Rajesh handles more pickup because my work can run late, and I handle morning food and schedule reminders.

follow_ups.question: What snacks do they reach for after school?
follow_ups.response: Neel wants anything filling: eggs, thepla, peanut butter toast. Maya likes fruit, yogurt, and sometimes leftover pasta.

follow_ups.question: Are they involved in Indian cultural activities too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially during festivals. Maya helps with art and flyers, and Neel helps set up chairs even if he complains.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My personal experiences have been mostly ordinary: traffic stops, community safety events, and police directing traffic at festivals. I have been pulled over twice in my life, once for speeding and once for a brake light, and both were okay though stressful. As a brown woman, I am aware that not everyone has the same experience. I tell my kids to be respectful and calm, but I also do not want them to think respect always protects you.

follow_ups.question: Have your children had direct experiences with police?
follow_ups.response: No serious ones. Mostly school resource officers and community events.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss police interactions at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially after news events. We talk about staying calm, knowing your rights, and calling us.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After 9/11, I remember more suspicion toward South Asian and Middle Eastern people generally. My family is Hindu Indian, but people do not always know the difference, and that period made many of us more cautious.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your daily behavior?
follow_ups.response: A little. My father was more careful about documents and travel, and we avoided arguments in public places.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel local police understood the community?
follow_ups.response: Some did, especially when they worked with community organizations. Others seemed distant.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate family has been arrested. I know of one distant family friend whose son had a DUI years ago, but that was not close to my household.

follow_ups.question: Did that distant case affect how you talked to your kids?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we used it as an example that one bad decision can follow you.

follow_ups.question: Any court involvement for your family?
follow_ups.response: No, nothing like that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in most elections, definitely presidential and midterms, and usually local elections too. Rajesh and I both vote, and we remind the kids that voting is part of living here. I did miss one small local election years ago because of a work emergency and felt annoyed with myself. I usually read local voter guides, especially for school board, judges, and millages.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in person or absentee?
follow_ups.response: Absentee lately, because my work schedule can change. I like filling it out at the kitchen table.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: With close friends, yes. In bigger community groups, I stay more careful because people can get heated.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am moderate Democrat, maybe practical liberal. I care about public schools, health care, immigration fairness, food safety, small business support, and treating working people with respect. I am not someone who likes slogans from either side. I want policies that actually work for families who are juggling kids, parents, bills, and jobs. Because I work in food service, I think a lot about wages, sick leave, and how people survive when hours are cut. Because my family is Indian-American, I care about immigration and about religious tolerance. I also believe in personal responsibility, and that comes from my upbringing. So I am progressive on inclusion and health care, practical on budgets, and impatient with political drama.

follow_ups.question: What issues most affect your vote?
follow_ups.response: Health care costs, education, reproductive rights, immigration policy, and whether candidates respect working families.

follow_ups.question: Are there any conservative views you hold?
follow_ups.response: I am careful with money and I believe people should work hard when they can. But I do not think that means abandoning people who need support.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more outspoken about health care and workers' rights since the pandemic. Before, I might have said, 'That is just politics.' But I saw food service and healthcare support workers treated as essential and still not always paid or protected properly. I also became more serious about school board races because misinformation started showing up locally. I am still moderate in how I talk, but I pay closer attention now.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic change how you saw your own job?
follow_ups.response: Yes. It made clear that feeding people in healthcare settings is part of care, not just a support service.

follow_ups.question: Do you donate or volunteer politically?
follow_ups.response: I have made small donations, but I do not campaign much. My volunteering is more community and cultural.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, so I do not pretend the experience is the same, but I do understand being seen as foreign or suspicious. Watching the videos and hearing Black coworkers talk about their fears made it more personal. It also made me examine anti-Black attitudes that can exist in South Asian communities. That part is uncomfortable but necessary.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about that inside your own community?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with close friends and with my children. In larger groups I choose my words carefully, but I do not stay silent if someone says something wrong.

follow_ups.question: Did coworkers influence your thinking?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Listening to Black coworkers describe worrying about their sons changed the conversation from abstract to human.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raised questions about accountability, dignity, and who gets believed. I do not agree with every phrase people use, but I understand why the anger exists. In my mind, supporting better policing and supporting communities should not be opposites. I want police trained well, held accountable, and not used as the answer to every social problem. I also think immigrant communities need to listen more and compare less.

follow_ups.question: What do you mean by compare less?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes immigrants say, 'We struggled too,' as if that cancels out someone else's history. It does not.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better de-escalation, transparent discipline, mental health responders, and real consequences for abuse.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think about race as something that shows up in daily life, not just big events. It shows up in schools, hiring, housing, who gets watched in stores, and whose accent is treated as smart or not smart. As an Indian-American, I have experienced bias, but I also know many Indian families have benefited from education and professional pathways that were not equally open to everyone. I want my children to be proud of being Indian and also aware of where they fit in a bigger American story.

follow_ups.question: How do you teach that to your children?
follow_ups.response: Through conversation, books, news, and correcting comments at home. I tell them pride should not become superiority.

follow_ups.question: Do you see race issues at work?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes in who gets promoted or who is assumed to be difficult. I try to be fair and very clear with expectations.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family, friends, and coworkers. I did not join large protests because of work and COVID concerns at the time, but I donated to local mutual aid and attended one community discussion online.

follow_ups.question: What conversations were hardest?
follow_ups.response: Conversations with older relatives who wanted to change the subject or say racism is only individual behavior.

follow_ups.question: Did your children respond differently than adults?
follow_ups.response: Yes, they were more direct and impatient. They pushed us to talk more openly.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Rajesh is thoughtful but quieter. Maya is very engaged and follows social justice issues online. Neel asks practical questions, like what he should do if a friend is treated unfairly. My friends are mixed. Some are active and outspoken, and some prefer not to discuss politics in community spaces. My Black coworkers were tired, honestly, and I tried to listen more than talk.

follow_ups.question: Has this caused conflict in your circle?
follow_ups.response: A little tension, mostly with older community members, but not major breakups.

follow_ups.question: Do you think your workplace handled it well?
follow_ups.response: They issued statements and did training, but real fairness depends on daily management, not posters.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall my health is good, but I am 51 and I feel my body more than I used to. I have mild high blood pressure that I manage with diet, exercise, and medication. My knees get sore from long shifts and jogging, so I have adjusted my workouts. Yoga helps my back and stress. I try to eat balanced meals, but working around food all day can be dangerous because tasting becomes snacking.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see a doctor?
follow_ups.response: At least annually, plus follow-ups for blood pressure every few months if medication changes.

follow_ups.question: What health habits are you most consistent about?
follow_ups.response: Yoga, walking, cooking at home, and keeping vegetables ready.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy because I know food, I like movement, and I have friends who exercise with me. It is hard because my job is physically tiring and full of tempting food. Stress also makes me want crunchy snacks at night. Winter in Michigan makes outdoor running harder.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you avoid for your blood pressure?
follow_ups.response: Too much salt, fried snacks, and heavy restaurant food. I still enjoy them, but not daily.

follow_ups.question: Who helps you stay active?
follow_ups.response: My yoga teacher, my dance group, and a running friend from my Chicago years who still checks in through our app.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: The main thing was my blood pressure creeping up and my doctor deciding I should start a low-dose medication. I did not love that, because I thought I could control everything with discipline, but it was the right choice. I also had knee pain last year after increasing jogging too quickly. Physical therapy taught me strengthening exercises, and now I am more careful. No broken bones or major surgery.

follow_ups.question: Did starting medication change how you saw yourself?
follow_ups.response: A little. I had to accept that being organized does not mean you can control genetics and age completely.

follow_ups.question: Are you still jogging?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but shorter runs, more walking intervals, and better shoes.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working or caring for my family, but knee pain can make a long shift harder. When it flares, I delegate lifting and take stretching breaks instead of trying to prove something.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable asking staff to help with lifting?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because I frame it as safety, not weakness.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for health recently?
follow_ups.response: Only routine appointments and one day when my knee was very swollen.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, mostly with my parents. My father has diabetes and some heart issues, and my mother has arthritis. I help schedule appointments and make food that fits his diet without making him feel punished. Rajesh's parents also have age-related health problems, but they are in New Jersey, so that is more phone coordination. Caring for elders is a real part of our life now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you take your parents to appointments?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month, depending on what is going on.

follow_ups.question: Does your brother help?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Amit helps with driving and paperwork. We divide it pretty well.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have insurance through Rajesh's job and some benefits through mine, so we are better off than many people. But deductibles, copays, and specialist scheduling are still frustrating. I have delayed physical therapy before because I wanted to see how much insurance would cover. Dental work for the kids also added up. We have not completely gone without necessary care, but we do time things around cost.

follow_ups.question: What care is hardest to schedule?
follow_ups.response: Specialists and physical therapy appointments that fit around work and school.

follow_ups.question: Do you understand your insurance bills easily?
follow_ups.response: No, and I am organized. The explanation of benefits can still feel like a puzzle.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, we use some Ayurvedic and home remedies, but alongside regular medicine, not instead of it. For colds we do ginger, turmeric, honey, ajwain steam, things like that. My mother believes strongly in certain foods for balance, and I respect that. But for blood pressure, diabetes, vaccines, infections, we use doctors and prescriptions. I do not play games with serious health.

follow_ups.question: What remedy do you use most often?
follow_ups.response: Ginger-tulsi tea with honey when someone has a sore throat.

follow_ups.question: Do your children accept those remedies?
follow_ups.response: They roll their eyes, but they drink the tea when they are sick.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I usually think of myself as a Democrat, but not blindly. I would say moderate Democrat. I vote Democratic most of the time because of health care, education, immigration, reproductive rights, and inclusion. But I still look at the person, especially in local races.

follow_ups.question: How strong is that identification?

follow_ups.question: Would you ever vote Republican?
follow_ups.response: For a local office maybe, if the person was competent and not extreme, but less likely now.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?

follow_ups.question: What pulls you that direction?
follow_ups.response: Health care, education, civil rights, and immigration.

follow_ups.question: What frustrates you about Democrats?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes too much messaging and not enough practical execution.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: Farmington Hills, Michigan.

follow_ups.question: Was that near where you live now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very close. I stayed connected to the area.

follow_ups.question: What was your high school environment like?
follow_ups.response: Suburban, competitive, and increasingly diverse.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, I lived with both my mother and father.

follow_ups.question: Were they strict?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially about school, friends, and being home on time.

follow_ups.question: Was the household close?
follow_ups.response: Very close, sometimes too close for a teenager.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: I lived with my younger brother Amit. Sometimes visiting relatives stayed with us for weeks.

follow_ups.question: Did extended family visits happen often?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially relatives from India or other states.

follow_ups.question: Did you share a room?
follow_ups.response: No, but space still felt shared because guests came often.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: My father completed a bachelor's degree in India.

follow_ups.question: What field was it in?
follow_ups.response: Commerce, from what he always told us.

follow_ups.question: Did he value education strongly?
follow_ups.response: Very strongly.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mother completed high school in India and some informal vocational training after coming here.

follow_ups.question: Did she want more schooling?
follow_ups.response: I think she did, but family and immigration life came first.

follow_ups.question: Did she push you academically?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in her own practical way.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, she worked for pay for many years.

follow_ups.question: Was she working when you were a teenager?
follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Did her work influence you?
follow_ups.response: Absolutely, especially my respect for food service workers.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in a school cafeteria. She helped prepare and serve meals, kept the line moving, cleaned, followed safety rules, and knew which children needed a little extra kindness. She was not a manager, but she had pride in doing things properly.

follow_ups.question: Did she cook similarly at home and work?
follow_ups.response: At home she was more creative; at work she followed menus and rules.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from watching her?
follow_ups.response: That feeding people is emotional labor as well as physical work.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a public school district cafeteria. They made breakfast and lunch for students, mostly standard school food, but the work mattered because kids needed to eat before learning.

follow_ups.question: Was it full time?
follow_ups.response: Mostly school-day hours, not year-round full time.

follow_ups.question: Did she like the schedule?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because it matched our school schedule better than many jobs.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked steadily.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, most of the time.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when I was younger.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked in purchasing and inventory for an auto parts supplier. He tracked parts, dealt with vendors, checked orders, and made sure production had what it needed. He was very detail-oriented, and I think I inherited that.

follow_ups.question: Did he talk about work at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly about suppliers, costs, and doing things correctly.

follow_ups.question: Did his work shape your inventory skills?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Counting and checking were normal in our house.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: It was an auto parts supply company connected to the Detroit automotive industry. They distributed parts and components to manufacturers and repair networks. In metro Detroit, that kind of work was everywhere.

follow_ups.question: Was his job stable?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, but the auto industry always had ups and downs.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect family finances?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes we were cautious because layoffs were always in the background.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope both children are doing well and still want to come home for dinner. I hope Rajesh and I are healthy and maybe able to travel more, especially to India, Italy, Japan, and Morocco. Professionally, I want to move into a kitchen manager role, maybe overseeing more than one location, and I want to complete a culinary arts or food service management certificate. I would love to develop a real staff training program, not just quick onboarding, because food service needs skilled leaders. The restaurant dream is still there: Indian-fusion, seasonal, beautiful plating, responsible sourcing. I do not know if it will become a full restaurant, catering concept, or teaching kitchen, but I want to build something with my name on it. I also hope to keep painting, dancing, and being part of the community without burning out.

follow_ups.question: What is the first concrete step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Choosing a certificate program and talking to my manager about advancement.

follow_ups.question: What would your dream restaurant serve?
follow_ups.response: Things like tandoori salmon with mango-chutney glaze, quinoa biryani with saffron, curried lentil risotto, and seasonal vegetable thalis.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, health, integrity, and hospitality. I value doing work properly, even when nobody is watching. I value culture, not as decoration, but as language, food, prayer, music, dance, and responsibility to others. I also value beauty: a well-plated dish, a watercolor wash, a sari color, a quiet museum room. And I value resilience, because most of life is not perfect timing; it is adjusting and still showing up.

follow_ups.question: Which value do you hope your children carry most?
follow_ups.response: Integrity with kindness. Being successful means little if you are careless with people.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel those values most clearly?
follow_ups.response: At my kitchen line during a hard service, at temple during Diwali, and at our dinner table on Sundays.
